Remove all other host plants from the field (e.g. castor bean).
Do not move cassava out of affected areas (consume locally)
During field work, wash hands, cloths and tools with soap/ bleach/ to remove virus
Monitoring: Monitor for the white flies that transmit cassava mosaic virus:
When leaves appear after planting, observe presence of white flies by shaking branches ; If 5– 10 infested plants are found per acre, consider action
Observe plants for disease symptoms once a week 2 to 3 months after planting:
Yellow spots on leaves; Misshaped leaves; Stunted growth; Rogue if less than 5% of plants show symptoms; If more than 5% of plants show
ACMV symptoms, do not rogue as disease spread can no longer be contained
Direct Control: Control white flies using liquid soap mixed with sugar or cooking oil.
Apply soap solution once per week (30 mls liquid soap /litre water or 5-8 g bar soap /litre water)
Seed extract: 50g/liter water with a little soap; Seed powder mix 1:1-1:2 with sawdust/soil; Leaves: 50-150g- 1-2 handful/ litre water, soap
Rogue (remove) and burn all infected plants.
Roguing is only effective when disease incidence is low (less than 5% of plants infected)
Restrictions: NOT ALLOWED in areas where cassava leaves are harvested for food, because leaf-picking persons may not know that a field has been sprayed.
There are no chemicals against viruses.
If virus symptoms are not yet apparent, you may spray against the white flies which vector
Once the virus is present in the crop, sprays against white flies are unlikely to be effective.

When using a pesticide, always wear protective clothing and follow the instructions on the product label, such as dosage, timing of application, pre- harvest interval, max number of sprays, restricted re-entry interval, min retreatment interval.
